paragraphs: The sale room of an old, famous firm of London book auctioneers is, of course, a great meeting place for collectors, librarians and dealers. That is true not only during auctions, but perhaps even more so when the books coming up for sale are on display. It was in such a room that a remarkable series of events began. Not many months ago, they were described to me by the person most directly affected: Mr. James Denton, Master of Arts, Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, and so on, formerly of Trinity Hall, and now, or until recently, of Rendcomb Manor in Warwickshire.

One spring day, not many years ago, he was spending a few days in London on business, mainly to do with furnishing the house he had just finished building at Rendcomb. You may be disappointed to learn that Rendcomb Manor was new. I cannot help that. There had indeed been an old house, but it was not especially beautiful or interesting. Even if it had been, neither beauty nor interest would have saved it from the disastrous fire that had burnt it to the ground about two years before this story begins. I am glad to say that all its most valuable contents had been saved, and that it was fully insured. Mr. Denton could therefore face the task of building a new, much more convenient home with a comparatively light heart. It was for himself and his aunt, who made up his entire household.

In London, with time to spare and not far from the sale room I have vaguely hinted at, Mr. Denton thought he would spend an hour there. He knew that part of the famous Thomas collection of manuscripts was on display. Perhaps he might find something about the history or geography of his part of Warwickshire.

Accordingly, he went in, bought a catalogue and went upstairs to the sale room. As usual, books were arranged in cases and spread out on the long tables. Many of the people standing at the shelves or sitting at the tables were familiar to him. He exchanged nods and greetings with several, then settled down to examine his catalogue and mark likely items. He had made good progress through about two hundred of the five hundred lots, occasionally getting up to take a volume from a shelf and glance through it, when someone laid a hand on his shoulder. He looked up. The man interrupting him was one of those intelligent men with pointed beards and flannel shirts whom the last quarter of the nineteenth century seems to me to have produced in such abundance.

I have no intention of repeating their entire conversation. It must be enough to say that it mostly concerned people they both knew. There was the nephew of Mr. Denton’s friend, who had recently married and settled in Chelsea; the friend’s sister-in-law, who had been seriously ill but was now better; and a piece of china the friend had bought some months earlier for far less than it was worth. You will rightly gather that the conversation was more of a monologue. In time, however, the friend remembered that Mr. Denton was there for a purpose. “What are you looking for in particular?” he asked. “I don’t think there’s much in this collection.” “Well, I thought there might be some Warwickshire collections, but I can’t see anything under Warwick in the catalogue.” “No, apparently not,” said the friend. “All the same, I believe I noticed something like a Warwickshire diary. What was the name? Drayton? Potter? Painter? A P or a D, I’m sure.” He quickly turned the pages. “Yes, here it is. Poynter. Lot 486. That might interest you. There are the books, I think, out on the table. Someone has been looking at them. Well, I must get on. Goodbye. You’ll come and see us, won’t you? Couldn’t you come this afternoon? We’re having a little music at about four. Well, then, next time you’re in town.” He left. Mr. Denton looked at his watch and found, to his dismay, that he had only a moment left before he must collect his luggage and catch his train. That moment was just enough to show him that the diary filled four fairly large volumes, covered the years around 1710, and seemed to contain a good many inserted items of various kinds. It seemed well worth leaving instructions to bid up to twenty-five pounds for it. He was able to do this, because his usual agent came into the room just as he was leaving.

That evening he rejoined his aunt at their temporary home, a small dower house a few hundred yards from the Manor. Next morning they resumed a discussion that had been going on for weeks about furnishing the new house. Mr. Denton gave his aunt an account of his visit to London, with details of carpets, chairs, wardrobes and bedroom china. “Yes, dear,” said his aunt, “but I don’t see any chintzes here. Did you go to ——?” Mr. Denton stamped on the floor. Where else, indeed, could he have stamped? “Oh dear, oh dear,” he said. “The one thing I forgot. I am sorry. The fact is, I was on my way there, and I happened to pass Robins’s.” His aunt threw up her hands. “Robins’s! Then the next thing will be another parcel of horrible old books at some outrageous price. I do think, James, when I’m taking all this trouble for you, you might manage to remember the one or two things I particularly begged you to see to. It’s not as if I were asking for myself. I don’t know whether you think I get any pleasure from it. If you do, I can assure you it’s quite the opposite. You have no idea of the thought and worry and trouble it causes me, and all you have to do is go to the shops and order things.” Mr. Denton interrupted with a repentant moan. “Oh, Aunt—” “Yes, that’s all very well, dear, and I don’t want to speak sharply, but you must know how very annoying it is. Particularly as it delays everything for I can’t tell how long. Today is Wednesday. The Simpsons come tomorrow, and you can’t leave them. Then on Saturday, as you know, we have friends coming for tennis. Yes, indeed, you spoke of inviting them yourself, though of course I had to write the notes. And it’s ridiculous to look like that, James. We must occasionally be civil to our neighbours. You wouldn’t like people to say we were perfect bears. What was I saying? Well, anyway, it comes to this: you can’t go to London again until Thursday next week at the earliest, and until we’ve decided on the chintzes, it’s impossible to settle one single other thing.”

Mr. Denton ventured to suggest that, since the paint and wallpaper were already settled, this was too harsh a view. But his aunt was not prepared to admit that just then. Indeed, there was nothing he could have suggested that she would have found herself able to accept. As the day went on, however, she moved back a little from this position. She examined her nephew’s samples and price lists with diminishing disapproval, and in some cases even gave his choices a cautious approval.

For his part, he was naturally rather downcast at having failed in his duty. He was still more depressed by the prospect of a lawn-tennis party, an unavoidable evil in August, but one he had thought he need not fear in May. He was somewhat cheered on Friday morning by the news that he had secured the four volumes of Poynter’s manuscript diary for twelve pounds and ten shillings. He was cheered still more when the diary itself arrived the following morning.

He had to take Mr. and Mrs. Simpson out for a drive in the car on Saturday morning and look after his neighbours and guests that afternoon. This prevented him from doing more than opening the parcel until everyone had gone to bed on Saturday night. Then he confirmed what he had previously only suspected: he had indeed acquired the diary of Mr. William Poynter, Squire of Acrington, about four miles from his own parish. This was the same Poynter who had once belonged to the circle of Oxford antiquaries centred on Thomas Hearne, and with whom Hearne apparently quarrelled in the end—not an uncommon event in that excellent man’s career. Like Hearne’s own collections, Poynter’s diary contained many notes from printed books, descriptions of coins and other antiquities brought to his attention, and drafts of letters about them, as well as the record of everyday events. The auction catalogue had given Mr. Denton no idea how much interesting material the book seemed to contain. He sat reading the first of the four volumes until a disgracefully late hour.

On Sunday morning, after church, his aunt came into the study. The sight of four brown leather quarto volumes on the table distracted her from what she had meant to say. “What are these?” she asked suspiciously. “New, aren’t they? Oh! Are these the things that made you forget my chintzes? I thought so. Disgusting. What did you pay for them, I should like to know? More than ten pounds? James, it’s really sinful. Well, if you have money to throw away on this sort of thing, there can be no reason why you shouldn’t contribute—and contribute generously—to my Anti-Vivisection League. There certainly can’t, James, and I shall be very seriously annoyed if—. Who did you say wrote them? Old Mr. Poynter of Acrington? Well, of course there is some interest in collecting old papers about this neighbourhood. But ten pounds!” She picked up one of the volumes, not the one her nephew had been reading, and opened it at random. The next instant she flung it to the floor with a cry of disgust as an earwig fell out from between the pages. Mr. Denton picked it up, muttering a suppressed curse. “Poor book!” he said. “I think you’re rather hard on Mr. Poynter.” “Was I, my dear? I beg his pardon, but you know I can’t bear those horrible creatures. Let me see whether I’ve done any damage.” “No, I think everything’s all right. But look what you’ve opened him at.” “Dear me, yes, of course! How very interesting. Unpin it, James, and let me look.”

It was a piece of patterned fabric about the size of the quarto page, fastened to it with an old-fashioned pin. James took it off and handed it to his aunt, carefully putting the pin back into the paper.

Now, I don’t know exactly what kind of fabric it was, but its printed design completely fascinated Miss Denton. She exclaimed in delight over it. She held it against the wall, then made James do the same so she could step back and study it from a distance. Next she examined it closely. She ended by praising, in the warmest terms, the taste of old Mr. Poynter, who had had the happy idea of keeping this sample in his diary. “It’s a most charming pattern,” she said, “and remarkable too. Look how delightfully the lines ripple, James. It reminds one very much of hair, doesn’t it? And then these knots of ribbon at intervals. They give exactly the touch of contrasting colour it needs. I wonder—” “I was going to say,” James put in deferentially, “I wonder whether it would cost much to have it copied for our curtains.” “Copied? How could you have it copied, James?” “Well, I don’t know the details. But I suppose it’s a printed pattern, and you could have a block cut from it in wood or metal.” “Now, really, that’s an excellent idea, James. I’m almost inclined to be glad that you were so—that you forgot the chintzes on Monday. At any rate, I promise to forgive and forget if you have this lovely old thing copied. Nobody will have anything remotely like it. And mind, James, we won’t allow it to be sold. Now I must go, and I’ve completely forgotten what I came in to say. Never mind, it will keep.”

After his aunt left, James Denton spent a few minutes examining the pattern more closely than he had yet had the chance to do. He was puzzled about why it had impressed Miss Denton so much. It did not seem especially remarkable or pretty to him. No doubt it was suitable enough for curtains. It ran in vertical bands, with some indication that these were meant to meet at the top. His aunt was right, too, that the main bands resembled rippling, almost curling locks of hair. Well, the chief thing was to find out, through trade directories or some other means, which firm would reproduce an old pattern like this. Rather than keep the reader waiting over this part of the story, I will say that he made a list of likely firms and chose a day to visit them, or some of them, with his sample.

His first two visits were unsuccessful, but there is luck in odd numbers. The third firm on his list, in Bermondsey, was used to this sort of work. The evidence they produced justified trusting them with the job. “Our Mr. Cattell” took an enthusiastic personal interest. “It’s heartrending, isn’t it, sir,” he said, “to think of the quantity of really lovely medieval material like this that lies almost unnoticed in so many of our country houses. Much of it, I take it, in danger of being thrown away as so much rubbish. What is it Shakespeare says? ‘Unconsidered trifles.’ Ah, I often say he has a word for us all, sir. I say Shakespeare, though I’m well aware not everyone agrees with me there. I had something of an upset the other day when a gentleman came in—a titled man, too, and I think he told me he’d written on the subject. I happened to quote something about Hercules and the painted cloth. Dear me, you never saw such a fuss. But as for this piece you’ve kindly entrusted to us, we shall take real enthusiasm in carrying out the work to the very best of our ability. What man has done, man can do, as I remarked only a few weeks ago to another valued client. In three to four weeks, all being well, we hope to put evidence of that before you, sir. Take the address, Mr. Higgins, if you please.”

That was the general drift of Mr. Cattell’s remarks at his first meeting with Mr. Denton. About a month later, after being told that some samples were ready to inspect, Mr. Denton met him again. He apparently had reason to be satisfied with how faithfully they had reproduced the design. They had finished it at the top as the pattern seemed to indicate, so that the vertical bands joined. But more work was needed to match the original colour. Mr. Cattell offered some technical suggestions that I need not trouble you with. His views about the pattern’s general appeal were also vaguely unfavourable. “You say you don’t want this supplied to anyone except personal friends with authorisation from you, sir. That shall be done. I quite understand your wish to keep it exclusive. It gives the suite a certain distinction, doesn’t it? What belongs to everyone belongs to no one, as they say.”
“Do you think it would be popular if anyone could buy it?” asked Mr. Denton.
“I hardly think so, sir,” said Cattell, thoughtfully clasping his beard. “I hardly think so. Not popular. It wasn’t popular with the man who cut the block, was it, Mr. Higgins?”
“Did he find it difficult to do?”

“He had no reason to, sir. But the fact is that the artistic temperament—and our men are artists, sir, every one of them, as truly artists as many to whom the world gives that title—is apt to develop some strange, almost unaccountable likes and dislikes. This was an example. The two or three times I went to inspect his progress, I could understand the bad language, because that’s his habit. But a real distaste for what I should call a pretty enough thing? I couldn’t understand that, and I still can’t.” Mr. Cattell looked closely at Mr. Denton. “It seemed as if the man scented something almost evil in the design.”
“Really? Did he tell you so? I can’t say I see anything sinister in it myself.”

“Neither can I, sir. In fact, I said as much. ‘Come, Gatwick,’ I said, ‘what’s the matter? What’s the reason for your prejudice? Because I can call it nothing more than that.’ But no, he gave no explanation. I was left, just as I am now, with a shrug of the shoulders and a ‘Who benefits?’ However, here it is.” With that, the conversation returned to the technical side of the matter.

Matching the colours of the background, the hem and the ribbon knots took by far the longest. It involved sending the original pattern and new samples back and forth many times. The Dentons were also away from the Manor during part of August and September. As a result, it was well into October before enough fabric had been made for curtains in the three or four bedrooms intended to have them.

On the feast of Saints Simon and Jude, the aunt and nephew returned from a short visit to find everything finished. They were delighted with the overall effect. The new curtains, in particular, looked wonderful in their surroundings. As Mr. Denton dressed for dinner and took stock of his room, where a great deal of the chintz was on display, he congratulated himself again and again on his luck. First it had made him forget his aunt’s errand, then it had put this extremely effective way of repairing his mistake into his hands. As he said at dinner, the pattern was so restful, yet so far from dull. Miss Denton, who had none of the fabric in her own room, was very much inclined to agree.

At breakfast next morning, he felt obliged to qualify his satisfaction a little, though only very slightly. “There’s one thing I rather regret,” he said. “We let them join the vertical bands of the pattern at the top. I think it would have been better to leave that alone.”
“Oh?” his aunt said questioningly.

“Yes. As I was reading in bed last night, they kept catching my eye. That is, I found myself looking across at them now and then. It gave the effect of someone repeatedly peeping out between the curtains, in one place or another, where there wasn’t an edge. I think that was because of the bands joining at the top. The only other thing that troubled me was the wind.”
“Why, I thought it was a perfectly still night.”
“Perhaps it was only on my side of the house, but there was enough to sway my curtains and rustle them more than I wanted.”

That night, an unmarried friend of James Denton’s came to stay. His room was on the same floor as his host’s, but at the far end of a long passage. Halfway along it stood a door covered in red baize, put there to stop draughts and block noise.

The three had gone their separate ways: Miss Denton well ahead of the others, and the two men at about eleven. James Denton did not yet feel ready for bed, so he sat in an armchair and read for a while. Then he dozed. When he woke, he remembered that his brown spaniel, which usually slept in his room, had not come upstairs with him. Then he thought he was mistaken. His hand hung over the arm of the chair within a few inches of the floor. As he happened to move it, he felt the faintest touch of hair against its back. He reached in that direction and stroked and patted something rounded. But the feel of it, and still more the way it remained absolutely still instead of moving in response, made him look over the arm of the chair. What he had been touching rose towards him. It was in the position of something that had crept along the floor on its belly, and as far as he could make out, it was a human figure. But the face now rising to within a few inches of his own had no visible features, only hair. Shapeless though it was, it carried such a dreadful air of menace that, as he leapt from the chair and rushed out of the room, he heard himself moaning with fear. No doubt he was right to flee. He dashed against the baize door that divided the passage and, forgetting it opened towards him, beat on it with all his strength. He felt a soft, ineffective tearing at his back. Yet it seemed to be growing stronger, as though the hand—or whatever was there that was worse than a hand—was becoming more solid as his pursuer’s rage grew more concentrated. Then he remembered how the door worked. He got it open. He shut it behind him. He reached his friend’s room. That is all we need to know.

It seems curious that, in all the time since buying Poynter’s diary, James Denton had not looked for an explanation of the pattern pinned inside it. Well, he had read through the diary without finding it mentioned, and had concluded that there was nothing to be said. But when he left Rendcomb Manor, not knowing whether he would ever return, he took the diary with him. He naturally insisted on leaving the day after the horror I have tried to describe. At his seaside lodgings he examined more closely the section from which the pattern had been taken. Something he remembered suspecting about it proved correct. Two or three leaves had been pasted together, but held up to the light, they could clearly be seen to have writing on them. Steam separated them easily, for the paste had lost much of its strength. They contained something relevant to the pattern.
The entry was written in 1707.

“Old Mr. Casbury of Acrington told me a great deal today about young Sir Everard Charlett. He remembered him as a fee-paying student at University College, and thought he belonged to the same family as Dr. Arthur Charlett, who is now Master of the College. Charlett was a handsome young gentleman, but a dissolute atheist and a great ‘lifter’, as they called heavy drinkers then, and may still do, for all I know. He was notorious, and was reprimanded at various times for his excesses. If the full history of his debauchery had been known, he would undoubtedly have been expelled from the College, unless someone had used their influence on his behalf. Mr. Casbury suspected that this had happened. He was a very beautiful man and always wore his own hair, which was remarkably abundant. Because of this and his dissolute life, his nickname was Absalom. He used to say that he did indeed believe he had shortened old David’s days, meaning his father, Sir Job Charlett, an honourable old Cavalier.

“Note that Mr. Casbury said he could not remember the year of Sir Everard Charlett’s death, but it was 1692 or 1693. He died suddenly in October. [Several lines describing his unpleasant habits and supposed offences are omitted.] Having seen him in such excellent spirits the night before, Mr. Casbury was astonished to hear of his death. He was found in the town ditch, with the hair, it was said, plucked clean off his head. Most of Oxford’s bells rang for him, because he was a nobleman, and he was buried the following night in St. Peter’s in the East. Two years later, however, when his successor was going to move him to his country estate, it was said that his coffin accidentally broke and proved completely full of hair. This sounds like a fable, but I believe earlier cases are on record, for instance in Dr. Plot’s History of Staffordshire.

“When his rooms were later stripped, Mr. Casbury acquired part of the wall hangings. It was said that Charlett had these designed expressly as a memorial to his hair, and gave the man who drew the pattern a lock to work from. The piece I have fastened here was part of those hangings, given to me by Mr. Casbury. He said he believed there was something subtle in the drawing, but he had never discovered it himself, nor had he much liked to study it closely.”

The money spent on the curtains might as well have been thrown into the fire, as the curtains were. Mr. Cattell’s comment on what he heard of the story was a quotation from Shakespeare. You may guess it easily enough. It began, “There are more things.”
